items.title: Temple Styles — Nagara, Dravida & Vesara
items.body:
### Indian temple styles

**In one line**
Indian temples are grouped into three classical styles — Nagara (North), Dravida (South) and Vesara (Deccan hybrid) — mainly by the shape of the tower over the shrine.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC repeatedly asks you to match a temple to its style/region, so you must link the tower shape and gateway type to the right part of India.

**The story**
Every temple is built around a tiny dark room, the **garbhagriha** ('womb-house'), which holds the main idol. Over time three regional ways of crowning and enclosing that room grew up. In the North the tower became a tall, curving spire; in the South it became a stepped pyramid inside a walled courtyard with giant gateway towers; in the Deccan the two ideas were deliberately mixed. The North Indian family also threw up a famous Odisha branch, the **Kalinga** sub-style, with its own beehive tower (deula) and a front hall (jagamohana).

**Why it matters**
The tower, gateway and enclosure are the quickest clues to date and place a temple, and they map onto the dynasties (Chandella, Chola, Hoysala, Eastern Ganga) that APPSC links to Andhra and South India.

**Picture it**

| Feature | Nagara (North) | Dravida (South) | Vesara (Deccan) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tower | curving, pointed **shikhara** | stepped, pyramidal **vimana** | mix of the two |
| Enclosure | usually no tall gateways | compound wall with **gopurams** | in-between |
| Examples | Kandariya Mahadeva (Khajuraho), Konark | Brihadeeswarar (Thanjavur), Meenakshi (Madurai) | Hoysaleswara (Halebidu) |

**Dravida phases (South):** Pallava (7th–9th c., rock-cut Mahabalipuram) → Chola (9th–13th c., giant vimana, Brihadeeswarar) → Pandya (13th–16th c., first great gopurams, Srirangam) → Vijayanagara (14th–17th c., colossal gopurams, Virupaksha at Hampi).

**Kalinga sub-style (Odisha):** beehive **deula** tower + front **jagamohana** hall — Lingaraj at Bhubaneswar (built by the Somavamsi rulers, 11th c.), Jagannath Puri (Eastern Ganga, 12th c.), Konark Sun Temple (Narasimhadeva I, 13th c.).

**Terms explained**
- **Garbhagriha** — the small, dark sanctum that holds the deity (literally 'womb-house').
- **Shikhara** — the North Indian temple tower (curving).
- **Vimana** — the South Indian temple tower (pyramidal, stepped).
- **Gopuram** — the tall ornate gateway tower in a South Indian temple's outer wall.
- **Mandapa** — a pillared hall in front of the sanctum for gatherings.
- **Deula / jagamohana** — the Odisha tower and its front assembly hall.

**Don't confuse**
- **Shikhara vs vimana** — shikhara is the North tower, vimana is the South tower; mixing these is the most common APPSC trap.
- **Gopuram vs vimana** — the gopuram is the gateway (on the wall); the vimana is over the shrine itself.

**Remember it**
'North Curves, South Pyramids, Deccan Mixes' — Nagara shikhara curves, Dravida vimana is a pyramid, Vesara mixes both.

**TL;DR**
- Nagara = curving shikhara, North India (Khajuraho, Konark).
- Dravida = pyramidal vimana + gopuram gateways, South India (Thanjavur, Madurai).
- Vesara = Nagara–Dravida hybrid, Deccan (Hoysala Belur/Halebidu).
- Kalinga (Odisha) = a Nagara sub-style with deula + jagamohana (Lingaraj, Konark).
keyPoints: Garbhagriha = sanctum; shikhara (North)/vimana (South) = sanctum tower; gopuram = South Indian gateway tower.
Nagara = curvilinear shikhara (North); Dravida = pyramidal vimana + gopuram enclosures (South); Vesara = hybrid of both (Deccan).
Kalinga (Odisha) sub-style: deula tower + jagamohana hall — Lingaraj, Jagannath Puri, Konark.
Dravida phases: Pallava (rock-cut) → Chola (giant vimana) → Pandya (gopurams) → Vijayanagara (colossal gopurams, Hampi).
Vesara/Hoysala temples (Belur, Halebidu) blend Nagara and Dravida forms in the Deccan.
items.mnemonic: 'North Curves, South Pyramids, Deccan Mixes' — Nagara shikhara curves, Dravida vimana is pyramidal, Vesara mixes.

items.title: Cave (Rock-cut) Architecture
items.body:
### Rock-cut cave architecture

**In one line**
Rock-cut caves are temples and monasteries carved directly into solid rock, used in turn by Buddhists, Jains and Hindus from the Mauryan age onward.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC asks who carved the earliest caves, the difference between a prayer hall and a monastery, and which site holds all three faiths — so the terms and the landmark sites must be clear.

**The story**
India's first caves were cut in the **Mauryan period**: the **Barabar Caves** near Gaya were given to the **Ajivika sect**, and the **Lomas Rishi** cave there is the oldest, its doorway copying wooden architecture. From the 2nd century BCE Buddhists cut two kinds of space — a **chaitya** (prayer hall built around a stupa) and a **vihara** (monastery with living cells). Later Jains and Hindus did the same, until at Ellora a Rashtrakuta king carved the Kailasa Temple out of a single hillside.

**Why it matters**
These caves preserve the earliest Indian architecture and painting, and the chaitya/vihara distinction is a favourite one-mark discriminator.

**Picture it**

| | Chaitya | Vihara |
|---|---|---|
| Use | prayer hall with a **stupa** | monastery / monks' residence |
| Plan | apsidal, arched (horseshoe) roof | cells around a central court |
| Example | Great Chaitya, Karla (Cave 8) | Ajanta, Kanheri viharas |

**Landmark sites:** Ajanta (Maharashtra) — 30 Buddhist caves, finest ancient fresco paintings, re-discovered 1819 by John Smith, UNESCO 1983. Ellora — 34 caves of all three faiths (17 Hindu, 12 Buddhist, 5 Jain), so Buddhist, Hindu and Jain rock-cut monuments stand together; a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1983); the Kailasa Temple, the largest monolithic excavation, by Rashtrakuta Krishna I. Elephanta (8th c., basalt) — Shaivite, famed Trimurti of Shiva, UNESCO 1987. Badami (Chalukya, 6th c.) — earliest Brahmanical cave paintings.

**Terms explained**
- **Rock-cut** — carved into living rock instead of built up from blocks.
- **Stupa** — a dome-shaped mound holding Buddhist relics.
- **Chaitya** — a Buddhist prayer hall centred on a stupa.
- **Vihara** — a Buddhist monastery with cells for monks.
- **Monolithic** — carved from one single piece of rock.

**Don't confuse**
- **Chaitya vs vihara** — chaitya is for prayer (has the stupa); vihara is for living (has cells). APPSC often swaps the two.
- **Ajanta vs Ellora** — Ajanta is famous for paintings and is all-Buddhist; Ellora is famous for carvings and has all three faiths.

**Remember it**
'A-E-E': Ajanta (paintings), Ellora (all faiths + Kailasa), Elephanta (Trimurti).

**TL;DR**
- Earliest caves = Mauryan Barabar (Ajivika sect); Lomas Rishi is the oldest.
- Chaitya = prayer hall with stupa (Karla); vihara = monastery with cells.
- Ajanta = Buddhist paintings (1819, UNESCO 1983); Ellora = all three faiths + Kailasa (Krishna I).
- Elephanta = Shaivite Trimurti (UNESCO 1987).
keyPoints: Earliest rock-cut caves = Mauryan Barabar Caves (Ajivika sect); Lomas Rishi is the oldest, copying timber architecture.
Chaitya = prayer hall with a stupa (Karla, Cave 8 = largest); Vihara = monastery with monks' cells.
Ajanta = 30 Buddhist caves, finest ancient frescoes, discovered 1819, UNESCO 1983.
Ellora has all three faiths (34 caves); Kailasa Temple = largest monolith, by Rashtrakuta Krishna I.
Elephanta (8th c.) is Shaivite, famed for the Trimurti of Shiva (UNESCO 1987).
items.mnemonic: 'A-E-E' painting-faiths-Trimurti: Ajanta (paintings), Ellora (all faiths + Kailasa), Elephanta (Trimurti).

items.title: Sculpture Schools, Pottery, Stupa & Ashokan Edicts
items.body:
### Sculpture schools, pottery, stupa and edicts

**In one line**
Around the 1st–3rd centuries CE three sculpture schools (Gandhara, Mathura, Amaravati) shaped the Buddha image, while pottery types and Ashokan pillars/edicts help date and read early India.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC loves to match a school to its stone/region, to ask the correct pottery sequence, and to test the scripts of Ashoka's edicts — Amaravati matters doubly because it is Andhra's own school.

**The story**
As Buddhism spread, artists in three regions began carving the Buddha. In the north-west, **Gandhara** sculptors trained in a Greco-Roman (Hellenistic) manner used grey schist — the Greek influence shows in wavy hair and toga-like robes. On the Yamuna, **Mathura** used local red sandstone in an indigenous style. On the Krishna delta in Andhra, the **Amaravati** school carved white marble narrative panels under Satavahana patronage. Meanwhile everyday pottery changed in a fixed order, and Ashoka published his moral messages on polished stone pillars, adapting the script to each region.

**Why it matters**
These are dating tools: pottery marks the stages of urbanisation, and the edicts show the reach of the Mauryan state and the spread of Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic.

**Picture it**

| School | Material / Trait | Patron / Region |
|---|---|---|
| Gandhara | grey schist, Greco-Roman Buddha | Kushana north-west |
| Mathura | indigenous red sandstone | Kushana, Yamuna |
| Amaravati | white marble narrative reliefs | Satavahana, Krishna delta (AP) |

**Pottery order:** OCP → PGW → NBPW (Ochre Coloured Ware → Painted Grey Ware → Northern Black Polished Ware). PGW belongs to the later-Vedic Ganga–Yamuna doab; NBPW is the luxury ware of the second urbanisation.

**Stupa parts:** the hemispherical **anda**, the **harmika** (railing on top), the **chhatra** (umbrella), and a boundary **vedika** (railing) pierced by **toranas** (gateways) — e.g. Sanchi and Amaravati.

**Ashokan pillars & edicts:** monolithic Chunar sandstone shafts with a mirror polish; the **Lion Capital at Sarnath** is India's national emblem (its Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes). Scripts/languages: Brahmi/Prakrit in the core, Kharoshthi/Aramaic in the north-west, Aramaic + Greek in Afghanistan.

**Terms explained**
- **Schist** — a layered grey stone used by Gandhara sculptors.
- **Relief** — a carving raised from a flat background.
- **Monolithic** — made from one single stone.
- **Capital** — the carved top of a pillar.
- **Torana** — a carved gateway in a stupa's railing.

**Don't confuse**
- **Gandhara vs Mathura** — Gandhara is grey schist + Greek look; Mathura is red sandstone + indigenous look.
- **Pottery order** — OCP is earliest and NBPW is latest; reversing them is the usual trap.

**Remember it**
'Old People Need' = OCP, PGW, NBPW (earliest to latest). Amaravati = Andhra's marble school.

**TL;DR**
- Gandhara = grey schist/Greek; Mathura = red sandstone/indigenous; Amaravati = white marble, Satavahana (AP).
- Pottery: OCP → PGW → NBPW (NBPW = second urbanisation).
- Stupa: anda, harmika, chhatra, vedika, torana.
- Ashokan pillars = polished Chunar sandstone; Sarnath Lion Capital = national emblem (24-spoke chakra).
keyPoints: Gandhara = Greco-Roman grey-schist Buddha; Mathura = indigenous red sandstone; Amaravati = white-marble reliefs under the Satavahanas (AP).
Pottery order: OCP → PGW → NBPW; NBPW is the deluxe ware of the second urbanisation.
Stupa parts: anda, harmika, chhatra, vedika (railing) and torana (gateway).
Ashokan pillars = monolithic Chunar sandstone with high polish; Lion Capital of Sarnath is the national emblem (Chakra = 24 spokes).
Ashokan edicts: Brahmi/Prakrit in the core, Kharoshthi/Aramaic in the north-west, Aramaic + Greek in Afghanistan.

items.title: Indo-Islamic Architecture
items.body:
### Indo-Islamic architecture

**In one line**
Indo-Islamic architecture is a blend of Indian building craft with Islamic arches and domes, producing mosques, tombs and forts in several regional styles.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC tests the trabeate-vs-arcuate difference, the signature features (charbagh, jaali, pietra dura), and the four regional styles with their monuments.

**The story**
When the Delhi Sultanate was set up in the early 13th century, Islamic builders brought the **arcuate** method — true arches and domes raised on wedge-shaped **voussoirs** — in place of India's older **trabeate** method of pillars, brackets and flat lintels. Because Islamic practice avoids living images, surfaces were covered with geometric patterns, flowing **arabesque** and **calligraphy**. Indian masons added their own stonework, lattice screens and later inlaid stone, and over three centuries four regional schools took shape.

**Why it matters**
This synthesis defines much of India's medieval heritage, including Andhra–Telangana's Qutb Shahi monuments, and it is a ready Mains example of cultural fusion.

**Picture it**

| Style | Example |
|---|---|
| Imperial (Delhi Sultanate) | Qutub Minar, Alai Darwaza, Quwwat-ul-Islam |
| Provincial | Atala Masjid (Jaunpur), Sidi Saiyyed jaalis (Gujarat), Bengal |
| Mughal | Humayun's Tomb, Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Fatehpur Sikri |
| Deccani | Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur), Charminar, Golconda |

Adhai Din Ka Jhopra (Ajmer) reused temple pillars — a provincial style using temple material; Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur, Deccani style) has a whispering gallery and a giant dome; the Taj Mahal at Agra is the Mughal masterpiece.

**Terms explained**
- **Trabeate** — built with pillars and flat beams/lintels (the older Indian way).
- **Arcuate** — built with arches and domes (the Islamic way).
- **Voussoir** — a wedge-shaped block that makes up an arch.
- **Charbagh** — a four-quartered garden symbolising paradise.
- **Jaali** — a pierced stone lattice screen.
- **Pietra dura** — inlay of semi-precious stones in marble.

**Don't confuse**
- **Trabeate vs arcuate** — pillars-and-beams vs arches-and-domes; this one word often decides the answer.
- **Imperial vs Mughal** — Qutub Minar is Sultanate (Imperial); the Taj Mahal is Mughal — do not swap them.
- **Not Indo-Islamic:** a curvilinear shikhara rising over the garbhagriha is a Hindu (Nagara) temple feature. Indo-Islamic buildings instead use the true arch, dome, minaret, jaali and calligraphy.

**Remember it**
'I-P-M-D' styles: Imperial, Provincial, Mughal, Deccani.

**TL;DR**
- Indo-Islamic = Indian trabeate craft + Islamic arcuate (arches/domes on voussoirs).
- Features: charbagh, jaali, pietra dura, calligraphy/arabesque, minars.
- Imperial = Qutub Minar; Mughal = Taj Mahal; Deccani = Gol Gumbaz, Charminar.
- Provincial = Jaunpur, Gujarat, Bengal.
keyPoints: Indo-Islamic = Indian trabeate + Islamic arcuate (arches/domes via voussoirs, squinches/pendentives).
Signature features: charbagh gardens, jaali screens, pietra dura inlay, calligraphy/arabesque, minars.
Imperial (Sultanate): Qutub Minar, Alai Darwaza; Mughal: Taj Mahal, Humayun's Tomb, Red Fort.
Provincial styles: Jaunpur (Atala Masjid), Gujarat (Sidi Saiyyed jaalis), Bengal.
Deccani style: Gol Gumbaz (whispering gallery, Bijapur), Charminar & Golconda (Hyderabad).

items.title: Painting, Colonial & Modern Architecture
items.body:
### Painting, colonial and modern architecture

**In one line**
This topic covers Indian painting (ancient frescoes and later miniatures), colonial building styles, and famous modern architects.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC asks which school a painting belongs to, which colonial power built in which style, and who designed Chandigarh or New Delhi.

**The story**
India's oldest surviving paintings are the Buddhist **frescoes** at Ajanta. Centuries later, royal courts produced small, detailed **miniatures** — the Mughal school peaking under the art-loving Jahangir, alongside Rajput and Pahari schools and the gold-leaf Tanjore panels of the South. When Europeans arrived they built in their own idioms: the Portuguese in Baroque, the French on grid plans, and the British first in Indo-Gothic, then in a fused Indo-Saracenic style, and finally in the Neo-Classical New Delhi of Lutyens and Baker. After independence, modern architects gave India new landmark cities and buildings.

**Why it matters**
These styles are visible across India (including French Yanam in AP) and give ready Mains examples of cultural contact and nation-building.

**Picture it**

| Architect | Signature |
|---|---|
| Le Corbusier | plan of Chandigarh, India's first planned city |
| Laurie Baker | 'Architect of the Poor', filler-slab eco housing, Kerala |
| Charles Correa | Jawahar Kala Kendra (Jaipur), MP Assembly; Padma Vibhushan 2006 |

**Painting:** Ajanta frescoes = finest ancient Buddhist murals; Bagh (MP) is a related, earthier tradition. Miniature schools: Mughal (zenith under Jahangir), Rajput/Rajasthani, Pahari (Basohli, Kangra); Tanjore uses gold foil and gesso.

**Colonial:** Portuguese Baroque (Basilica of Bom Jesus, Goa); French Cartesian grid towns (Puducherry, Yanam in AP); British Indo-Gothic (Victoria Memorial, Gateway of India, CSMT Mumbai), Indo-Saracenic (Indian domes/chhatris/jaalis on Gothic frames), and post-1911 Neo-Classical New Delhi (Lutyens & Herbert Baker; Rashtrapati Bhavan's 'upturned' dome).

**Terms explained**
- **Fresco** — a wall painting done on fresh plaster.
- **Miniature** — a small, highly detailed court painting.
- **Indo-Saracenic** — a colonial revival fusing Indian features with European Gothic/Classical.
- **Neo-Classical** — a revival of Greek/Roman columns and symmetry.

**Don't confuse**
- **Indo-Gothic vs Indo-Saracenic** — Indo-Gothic is European Gothic in India (CSMT); Indo-Saracenic adds Indian domes and chhatris onto it.
- **Le Corbusier vs Correa** — Le Corbusier planned Chandigarh; Correa designed Jawahar Kala Kendra.

**Remember it**
Jahangir = the connoisseur, so Mughal miniatures peak under him; Le Corbusier = Chandigarh.

**TL;DR**
- Ajanta = finest ancient frescoes; Mughal miniatures peak under Jahangir; Rajput/Pahari/Tanjore are other schools.
- British colonial: Indo-Gothic, Indo-Saracenic, Neo-Classical New Delhi (Lutyens & Baker).
- French used grid town planning (Puducherry, Yanam in AP).
- Le Corbusier = Chandigarh; Laurie Baker = 'Architect of the Poor'; Correa = Padma Vibhushan (2006).
keyPoints: Ajanta = finest ancient frescoes; Mughal miniatures peaked under Jahangir; Rajput, Pahari (Kangra/Basohli) and Tanjore are other schools.
British colonial: Indo-Gothic (Victoria Memorial, Gateway of India, CSMT), Indo-Saracenic, and post-1911 Neo-Classical New Delhi (Lutyens & Baker).
French colonial architecture used Cartesian grid town planning (Puducherry, Yanam in AP).
Le Corbusier planned Chandigarh; Laurie Baker = 'Architect of the Poor' (filler slab); Charles Correa won the Padma Vibhushan (2006).
Vidhana Soudha (Bengaluru) is Neo-Dravidian; Lotus Temple is a modern Bahá'í house of worship.

items.title: UNESCO Sites of India & Andhra Pradesh Art
items.body:
### UNESCO sites of India and Andhra art

**In one line**
India's UNESCO World Heritage Sites are its globally recognised cultural and natural treasures, and Andhra Pradesh adds its own Buddhist and temple heritage to this list.

**Why it is asked**
Current-affairs style questions ask the latest inscription and the total count, while AP-focused questions test Amaravati, Lepakshi and Srisailam.

**The story**
UNESCO lists sites of 'outstanding universal value'. India's first four were inscribed together in 1983, and the list has grown steadily, with new sites added almost every year. Andhra's contribution runs from the Satavahana-era marble Buddhist art of Amaravati, through the Ikshvaku remains at Nagarjunakonda, to the Vijayanagara murals of Lepakshi and the great Dravidian temples at Srisailam and Tirupati.

**Why it matters**
The newest inscriptions are easy current-affairs marks, and the AP sites tie this topic to the state-specific weighting APPSC gives.

**Picture it**

| Site | Year |
|---|---|
| Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas; Santiniketan | 2023 |
| Moidams (Charaideo, Assam — Ahom mounds) | 2024 |
| Maratha Military Landscapes of India | 2025 |
| Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath (latest) | 2026 |

India has 45 sites as of 2026 — 37 cultural, 7 natural, 1 mixed (Khangchendzonga NP) — and ranks 6th worldwide. The first four (1983) were Ajanta Caves, Ellora Caves, Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal.

**AP art:** Amaravati school of sculpture (white-marble Buddhist reliefs on the Krishna river, patronised by the Satavahanas); Nagarjunakonda Buddhist remains; Lepakshi Veerabhadra temple (Vijayanagara) with its hanging pillar and ceiling murals; Srisailam (Mallikarjuna) and Tirupati Dravidian temples.

**Terms explained**
- **World Heritage Site** — a place UNESCO lists as having outstanding universal value.
- **Cultural / natural / mixed** — whether a site is valued for human works, nature, or both.
- **Inscription** — the act of adding a site to the UNESCO list.

**Don't confuse**
- **Moidams vs Maratha Landscapes** — Moidams (Assam) came in 2024; the Maratha Military Landscapes in 2025.
- **Amaravati school vs Amaravati city** — the school is the Buddhist marble art; it is separate from the modern AP capital area.

**Remember it**
First four of 1983 = 'A-E-A-T': Ajanta, Ellora, Agra Fort, Taj Mahal.

**TL;DR**
- India = 45 UNESCO sites in 2026 (37 cultural, 7 natural, 1 mixed).
- First four (1983): Ajanta, Ellora, Agra Fort, Taj Mahal.
- Recent: Moidams (2024), Maratha Military Landscapes (2025), Sarnath (2026, latest).
- AP art: Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Lepakshi, Srisailam.
keyPoints: India has 45 UNESCO World Heritage Sites as of 2026 (37 cultural, 7 natural, 1 mixed — Khangchendzonga).
The first four Indian sites (1983) were Ajanta, Ellora, Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal.
Maratha Military Landscapes of India was inscribed in 2025; the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath (2026) is the latest.
Moidams (Charaideo, Assam) was inscribed in 2024 — the first cultural site from the North-East.
AP art: Amaravati marble Buddhist school (Satavahana), Lepakshi's hanging pillar & murals, Srisailam Dravidian temple.

items.title: Temple Vocabulary, Nagara Sub-types and Odisha — Detail
items.body:
### Temple Vocabulary, Nagara Sub-types and Odisha — Detail

**In one line**
The words examiners use for temple parts, the three kinds of Nagara tower, and the landmark north-Indian and Odishan temples.

**The story**
A temple is read from the inside out: sanctum, **antarala**, mandapa, and around them the **pradakshina** path; in front stand the **vahana** and the **dhvaja** stambha. A Nagara tower ends in the **amalaka** and **kalasha**. Its tower comes in three types — **latina**, **phamsana** and **valabhi**. Early Gupta temples show the growth: flat-roofed **Temple 17** at Sanchi, brick **Bhitargaon**, and the **panchayatana** at **Deogarh**. In the 10th–11th centuries the **Chandela** kings built Khajuraho; the Solanki **Bhima I** built **Modhera**, and his minister **Vimal** Shah began the **Dilwara** shrines. In Odisha the vocabulary is **rekha deula**, **pidha deula**, **khakhara** and **natamandira**. Puri was built by **Anantavarman Chodaganga**, and Konark is the **Black Pagoda** with **24 wheels**. **Rajarani** has no deity, and **Mukteshwar** is the gem of the style. Two later events shaped north Indian temples. Mahmud sacked **Somnath** in **1026**, and **Ahilyabai Holkar** rebuilt Kashi Vishwanath in **1780**.

#### Temple terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Pradakshina path** | Circumambulatory passage round the sanctum |
| **Antarala** | Antechamber between sanctum and hall |
| **Vahana** | The deity's mount, facing the sanctum |
| **Dhvaja stambha** | Flagstaff before the sanctum |
| **Garuda stambha** | Pillar bearing the mount of Vishnu |
| **Amalaka** | Ribbed stone disc atop a Nagara shikhara |
| **Kalasha** | Pot-shaped finial at the top of the tower |
| **Panchayatana** | Main shrine with four corner shrines |
| **Jagati** | Raised platform under the temple |
| **Yajna kund** | Sacred fire pit near the temple |

#### Nagara types and temples

| Type / temple | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Latina / rekha-prasada** | Simple curvilinear Nagara shikhara |
| **Phamsana** | Broad, short, stepped-slab roof (often over mandapas) |
| **Valabhi** | Rectangular plan, barrel-vaulted roof |
| **Dashavatara temple, Deogarh** | Gupta (c. 500 CE) panchayatana with an early shikhara |
| **Bhitargaon** | Gupta brick temple (Kanpur) |
| **Temple 17, Sanchi** | Early flat-roofed Gupta temple |
| **Khajuraho temples** | Chandela dynasty, 10th–11th century |
| **Modhera Sun Temple** | Solanki king Bhima I, 1026 — stepped Surya Kund |
| **Dilwara temples, Mount Abu** | Marble Jain temples — Vimal Vasahi (1031) of Vimal Shah |
| **Kashi Vishwanath (present temple)** | Rebuilt 1780 by Ahilyabai Holkar |
| **Somnath temple** | Sacked by Mahmud of Ghazni, 1026 |

#### Kalinga (Odisha)

| Element / temple | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Rekha deula** | Tall curvilinear tower over the sanctum |
| **Pidha deula** | Pyramidal tiered roof of the jagamohana |
| **Khakhara deula** | Barrel-roofed type — Vaital Deul |
| **Natamandira** | Dance hall in front of the jagamohana |
| **Jagannath temple, Puri** | Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva, 12th century |
| **Konark Sun Temple** | 'Black Pagoda' — chariot of 24 wheels, 7 horses |
| **Rajarani temple** | No deity in the sanctum (11th c.) |
| **Mukteshwar temple** | 'Gem of Odishan architecture' — torana arch |

**Don't confuse**
- **Amalaka** (ribbed disc) sits **below** the **kalasha** (pot finial) on a Nagara shikhara.
- **Rekha deula** = sanctum tower; **pidha deula** = jagamohana roof — both Odishan terms.
- **Modhera** (Solanki, Gujarat) ≠ **Konark** (Eastern Ganga, Odisha) — both Sun temples.

**TL;DR**
- Terms: pradakshina, antarala, vahana, dhvaja, amalaka + kalasha, panchayatana, jagati.
- Nagara towers: latina, phamsana, valabhi; Gupta: Sanchi 17, Bhitargaon, Deogarh.
- Chandela Khajuraho; Modhera (Bhima I, 1026); Dilwara (Vimal Vasahi 1031); Somnath sacked 1026; Kashi rebuilt 1780.
- Odisha: rekha/pidha/khakhara deula, natamandira; Puri (Chodaganga); Konark Black Pagoda (24 wheels); Rajarani; Mukteshwar.
keyPoints: The amalaka is the ribbed stone disc at the top of a Nagara shikhara.
The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh is a Gupta panchayatana temple.
The Modhera Sun Temple was built by the Solanki king Bhima I.
Konark Sun Temple is called the Black Pagoda.

items.title: Dravida and Vesara Temples — Detail
items.body:
### Dravida and Vesara Temples — Detail

**In one line**
The Pallava, Chola, Nayaka and Vijayanagara landmarks of the south, and the Chalukya, Hoysala and Kakatiya temples of the Deccan.

**The story**
Dravida temples sit inside **prakara** walls guarded by **dvarapala** figures. Vijayanagara added the **kalyana mandapa** and the **amman** shrine. The Pallavas moved from **Mandagapattu** and the **Pancha Rathas** of **Narasimhavarman I** to **Rajasimha**'s structural Shore Temple, and carved **Arjuna's Penance**. **Vaikuntha Perumal** was Nandivarman II's. The Cholas built big: **Rajaraja I** finished Thanjavur in **1010**, **Rajendra I** built Gangaikondacholapuram, and **Rajaraja II** built **Darasuram**. Their **Nataraja** bronzes were cast by the **lost-wax** method. Later came the **Nayaka** Meenakshi temple, Rameswaram's **longest** corridor and Srirangam's **seven prakaras**. At Hampi stand the **Vittala** temple's **stone chariot** and **musical pillars**, the **Hazara Rama** chapel and the **raya gopuram**s. In the Deccan, **Aihole** is the **cradle** of temple building (its Durga temple is **apsidal**). At Pattadakal, **Lokamahadevi**'s Virupaksha stands beside the Nagara **Papanatha**; the Badami caves were cut under **Mangalesha**. Hoysala temples are **star-shaped** and carved in **soapstone**. **Vishnuvardhana** built Belur in **1117**; **Dorasamudra** (Halebidu) and **Somanathapura** followed. The Kakatiyas gave **Rudradeva**'s Thousand Pillar temple and **Recherla Rudra**'s Ramappa (**1213**). The **Navabrahma** temples of Alampur carry Nagara towers deep in the south.

#### Dravida

| Element / temple | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Prakara** | Concentric enclosure walls |
| **Kalyana mandapa** | Hall for the deity's wedding — Vijayanagara |
| **Amman shrine** | Separate shrine for the consort goddess |
| **Dvarapala** | Door-guardian figures |
| **Mandagapattu** | Mahendravarman I's first Pallava rock-cut shrine |
| **Pancha Rathas** | Monoliths of Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) |
| **Arjuna's Penance** | Open-air rock relief, Mahabalipuram |
| **Shore Temple & Kailasanatha (Kanchi)** | Rajasimha (Narasimhavarman II), 8th c. |
| **Vaikuntha Perumal, Kanchipuram** | Nandivarman II |
| **Brihadeeswarar, Thanjavur** | Rajaraja I, completed 1010 |
| **Gangaikondacholapuram temple** | Rajendra I — Ganga expedition |
| **Airavatesvara, Darasuram** | Rajaraja II |
| **Chola bronzes (Nataraja)** | Lost-wax (cire perdue) casting |
| **Meenakshi temple, Madurai** | Nayaka (17th c.) — Hall of a Thousand Pillars |
| **Ramanathaswamy, Rameswaram** | Longest temple corridor in India |
| **Ranganathaswamy, Srirangam** | Seven prakaras — the largest functioning temple complex |
| **Vittala temple, Hampi** | Stone chariot and musical pillars |
| **Hazara Rama temple** | Royal chapel with Ramayana friezes |
| **Raya gopurams** | Krishnadevaraya's colossal gateways |

#### Vesara and Deccan

| Temple / feature | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Aihole** | 'Cradle of Indian temple architecture' |
| **Durga temple, Aihole** | Apsidal (gajaprishtha) plan |
| **Virupaksha temple, Pattadakal** | Queen Lokamahadevi — Vikramaditya II's Pallava victory |
| **Papanatha temple, Pattadakal** | Nagara-mode temple beside Dravida ones |
| **Badami cave temples** | Excavated under Mangalesha (Chalukya) |
| **Hoysala temple plan** | Star-shaped jagati; soapstone carving |
| **Chennakeshava, Belur** | Vishnuvardhana, 1117 |
| **Halebidu** | Hoysala capital Dorasamudra (Hoysaleswara temple) |
| **Keshava temple, Somanathapura** | Late Hoysala, 1268 |
| **Ramappa temple, Palampet** | Recherla Rudra, 1213 (Kakatiya Ganapatideva) |
| **Thousand Pillar temple, Hanamkonda** | Kakatiya Rudradeva, 1163 |
| **Alampur temples** | Navabrahma group — Nagara shikharas of the Badami Chalukyas |

**Don't confuse**
- **Narasimhavarman I** = Pancha Rathas (monolithic); **Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha)** = Shore Temple (structural).
- **Rajaraja I** = Thanjavur (1010); **Rajendra I** = Gangaikondacholapuram; **Rajaraja II** = Darasuram.
- **Ramappa** (Recherla Rudra, 1213) ≠ **Thousand Pillar temple** (Rudradeva, 1163) — both Kakatiya, both now in Telangana.

**TL;DR**
- Dravida terms: prakara, kalyana mandapa (Vijayanagara), amman shrine, dvarapala.
- Pallava: Mandagapattu → Pancha Rathas (Narasimhavarman I) → Shore Temple & Kailasanatha (Rajasimha); Arjuna's Penance.
- Chola: Thanjavur (Rajaraja I, 1010), Gangaikondacholapuram (Rajendra I), Darasuram (Rajaraja II); lost-wax Nataraja.
- Deccan: Aihole cradle; Pattadakal (Lokamahadevi; Papanatha); Badami (Mangalesha); Hoysala star plan, soapstone; Belur 1117; Ramappa 1213; Alampur Navabrahma.

The Pancha Rathas were carved under Narasimhavarman I.
Rajaraja I completed the Brihadeeswarar temple in 1010.
Hoysala temples have a star-shaped plan and are carved in soapstone.
The Ramappa temple was built in 1213 by Recherla Rudra.

items.title: More Rock-cut Caves — Detail
items.body:
### More Rock-cut Caves — Detail

**In one line**
Beyond Ajanta and Ellora: the paintings, patrons and faiths of India's other cave sites, including two in Andhra.

**The story**
At Ajanta, Cave 1 holds the **Padmapani**, and the later caves were cut under **Vakataka** patronage. Ellora — **Verul** Leni — has Jain caves too, the **Indra Sabha** group. Elephanta is carved in **basalt**. The Mauryan Barabar hills hold the Lomas Rishi, **Sudama** and two more caves. At the Nagarjuni hills **Dasharatha** gave caves to the Ajivikas. The **Bagh** caves have earthy tempera murals. In the Western Ghats the Buddhist caves of **Bhaja**, Karle, **Kanheri** and Nashik (**Pandav Leni**) are found; **Mandapeshwar** later became a church. Hindu and Jain caves include the **Varaha** relief at Udayagiri near Vidisha, and **Kharavela**'s **Khandagiri**–Udayagiri in Odisha. In Andhra, **Undavalli** has a reclining Vishnu, **Guntupalli** has a round rock-cut chaitya, and the **Borra** caves near Araku are natural limestone caverns.

#### Caves

| Cave | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Padmapani** | Bodhisattva painting, Ajanta Cave 1 |
| **Later Ajanta caves** | Vakataka patronage (Harishena) |
| **Ellora** | Also called 'Verul Leni' |
| **Indra Sabha & Jagannatha Sabha** | Jain caves at Ellora |
| **Elephanta caves** | Cut in basalt; Buddhist before Shaivite |
| **Barabar group** | Lomas Rishi, Sudama, Vishwakarma, Karan Chaupar |
| **Nagarjuni caves** | Dasharatha (Ashoka's grandson) — for Ajivikas |
| **Bagh caves** | MP, 6th c. — earthy tempera paintings |
| **Nashik caves** | 'Pandav Leni' — 24 Hinayana caves |
| **Mandapeshwar cave** | Brahmanical, later Christian (Borivali) |
| **Bhaja** | Early Western-Ghats chaitya |
| **Kanheri** | 100+ Buddhist caves, Mumbai |
| **Udayagiri caves, Vidisha** | Chandragupta II — Varaha relief |
| **Udayagiri–Khandagiri (Odisha)** | Early Jain rock-cut shelters — Kharavela's age |
| **Guntupalli (AP)** | Circular rock-cut Buddhist chaitya |
| **Undavalli caves (AP)** | Reclining Vishnu — Vishnukundin era |
| **Borra caves (AP)** | Natural limestone caves — Araku valley |

**Don't confuse**
- **Udayagiri (Vidisha, MP)** = Gupta, Varaha; **Udayagiri–Khandagiri (Odisha)** = Jain, Kharavela.
- **Barabar** (Ashoka) and **Nagarjuni** (Dasharatha) caves were both for the **Ajivikas**.
- **Borra** caves are **natural**, not rock-cut.

**TL;DR**
- Ajanta: Padmapani (Cave 1), Vakataka patronage; Ellora = Verul, Jain Indra Sabha; Elephanta basalt.
- Barabar: Lomas Rishi, Sudama, Vishwakarma, Karan Chaupar; Nagarjuni: Dasharatha.
- Bagh (tempera); Bhaja, Kanheri, Nashik (Pandav Leni), Mandapeshwar.
- Udayagiri Vidisha (Varaha); Udayagiri–Khandagiri (Kharavela); AP: Undavalli reclining Vishnu, Guntupalli circular chaitya, Borra natural caves.
keyPoints: The Padmapani painting is in Ajanta Cave 1.
The Nagarjuni caves were given to the Ajivikas by Dasharatha.
The Udayagiri caves near Vidisha are famous for the Varaha relief.
Guntupalli in Andhra Pradesh has a circular rock-cut chaitya.

items.title: Sculpture Landmarks, Pottery Types and Inscriptions — Detail
items.body:
### Sculpture Landmarks, Pottery Types and Inscriptions — Detail

**In one line**
The famous pieces from Harappa to Santiniketan, three more pottery types, and the inscriptions every exam asks about.

**The story**
Indian sculpture runs from the **Dancing Girl** and the **steatite** priest-king of the Indus cities, through the polished **Didarganj** Yakshi and the **Dhauli** elephant of Mauryan times, to the Gupta Sarnath Buddhas with **transparent drapery**, and finally to the modern **Ramkinkar Baij**. Pottery adds **Black and Red Ware**, Kushana **Red Polished Ware** and the **Blue pottery** of **Jaipur**. Ashoka's edicts carry distinct messages: **XIII** on **Kalinga**, **Major Rock Edict II** on the south, V on the **Dhamma Mahamatras** and **XII** on tolerance. Pillars at **Rummindei** and **Nigali Sagar** mark Buddhist sites. **Maski** first names Ashoka, and **Kalsi** has all fourteen edicts. **Shahbazgarhi** is in Kharoshthi and **Kandahar** in Greek and Aramaic. Other inscriptions name kings and deeds: **Sohgaura**, the **Mehrauli** pillar, **Harisena** on the Allahabad pillar, **Ravikirti** at Aihole, **Rudradaman** at Junagadh (the **Sudarshana** lake), **Gautami Balashri** at Nasik, **Hathigumpha**, **Heliodorus** at Besnagar, **Naganika** at Naneghat, **Halmidi**, **Talagunda**, **Kudumiyanmalai**, **Uttaramerur** and **Mihira Bhoja** at Gwalior. Andhra's **Bhattiprolu** caskets carry south India's earliest Brahmi.

#### Sculpture and pottery

| Piece / ware | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Dancing Girl** | Bronze, lost-wax — Mohenjodaro |
| **Priest-king bust** | Steatite — Mohenjodaro |
| **Didarganj Yakshi** | Polished Mauryan sandstone chauri-bearer |
| **Dhauli** | Rock-cut elephant beside an edict |
| **Sarnath (Gupta) Buddha** | Transparent drapery, ornate halo |
| **Ramkinkar Baij** | Pioneer of modern Indian sculpture (Santiniketan) |
| **Black and Red Ware** | Chalcolithic–megalithic pottery |
| **Red Polished Ware** | Kushana period, stamped designs |
| **Blue pottery** | Jaipur — Persian/Turko-Mughal origin |

#### Edicts and inscriptions

| Inscription | Content |
|---|---|
| **Major Rock Edict XIII** | Kalinga war and Ashoka's remorse |
| **Major Rock Edict II** | Southern kingdoms; medical care |
| **Major Rock Edict V** | Appointment of Dhamma Mahamatras |
| **Major Rock Edict XII** | Tolerance among sects |
| **Rummindei pillar** | Visit to Lumbini; tax relief |
| **Nigali Sagar pillar** | Stupa of Kanakamuni enlarged |
| **Maski edict** | First to name Ashoka |
| **Kalsi** | All 14 major rock edicts (north India) |
| **Shahbazgarhi & Mansehra** | Edicts in Kharoshthi |
| **Kandahar edict** | Greek–Aramaic bilingual |
| **Sohgaura copper plate** | Famine relief, pre-Ashokan Brahmi |
| **Mehrauli iron pillar** | Rust-free; King Chandra (Chandragupta II) |
| **Allahabad pillar** | Ashoka + Harisena's prashasti + Jahangir |
| **Aihole inscription** | Ravikirti — Pulakeshin II defeats Harsha |
| **Junagadh (Girnar) inscription** | Rudradaman — Sudarshana lake repairs |
| **Nasik inscription** | Gautami Balashri on Gautamiputra Satakarni |
| **Hathigumpha inscription** | Kharavela's year-by-year record |
| **Besnagar Garuda pillar** | Greek envoy Heliodorus — Vasudeva |
| **Bhattiprolu inscription (AP)** | Earliest Brahmi of south India |
| **Naneghat inscription** | Queen Naganika's sacrifices |
| **Halmidi inscription** | Earliest Kannada record (c. 450) |
| **Talagunda inscription** | Origin of the Kadambas (Mayurasharman) |
| **Kudumiyanmalai inscription** | Musical notation (Pallava) |
| **Uttaramerur inscription** | Chola village-assembly elections (Parantaka I) |
| **Gwalior inscription** | Pratihara Mihira Bhoja |

**Don't confuse**
- **Junagadh/Girnar**: **Rudradaman** (first long Sanskrit inscription) repaired the Sudarshana lake; Skandagupta repaired it again.
- **Hathigumpha** (Kharavela, Odisha) ≠ **Nasik** (Gautami Balashri, Satavahana).
- **Maski** = first to name Ashoka; **Kalsi** = all 14 major rock edicts in the north.

**TL;DR**
- Sculpture: Dancing Girl (bronze), steatite priest-king, Didarganj Yakshi, Dhauli elephant, Gupta Sarnath, Ramkinkar Baij.
- Pottery: BRW (Chalcolithic), RPW (Kushana), Blue pottery (Jaipur).
- Ashoka: MRE II (south), V (Mahamatras), XII (tolerance), XIII (Kalinga); Rummindei, Nigali Sagar, Maski, Kalsi, Shahbazgarhi (Kharoshthi), Kandahar (Greek-Aramaic).
- Other: Sohgaura, Mehrauli, Allahabad (Harisena), Aihole (Ravikirti), Junagadh (Rudradaman), Nasik, Hathigumpha, Besnagar, Naneghat, Halmidi, Talagunda, Kudumiyanmalai, Uttaramerur; AP Bhattiprolu.
keyPoints: Major Rock Edict XIII describes the Kalinga war.
The Maski edict was the first to name Ashoka.
Harisena's prashasti of Samudragupta is on the Allahabad pillar.
The Bhattiprolu inscriptions are the earliest Brahmi records of south India.
The Halmidi inscription is the earliest Kannada record.

items.title: Indo-Islamic Monuments and Their Builders — Detail
items.body:
### Indo-Islamic Monuments and Their Builders — Detail

**In one line**
Who built what, from the first mosque in Delhi to the last Mughal garden tomb, with the Deccan landmarks of Hyderabad.

**The story**
The Sultanate began with the **Quwwat-ul-Islam** mosque and the Qutub Minar, completed by **Iltutmish**. The **Alai Darwaza** carried the first **true arch** and dome. Tughlaq buildings have **sloping** walls, and Firoz Shah's **Hauz Khas** and the **Khirki** mosque followed. Provincial schools gave the **Sharqi** mosques of Jaunpur, **Hoshang Shah**'s marble tomb at Mandu and the **Adina** Mosque of Bengal. In the Deccan, **Mahmud Gawan**'s madrasa stands at Bidar. Hyderabad has the **Mecca Masjid**, and Golconda its **acoustic** fort. The Mughals began with **Mirak Mirza Ghiyas**'s **double dome** at Humayun's tomb. Akbar built the **Buland Darwaza** and **Panch Mahal**; Nur Jahan the **Baby Taj**. **Ustad Ahmad Lahori** designed the Taj, and Shah Jahan finished the Red Fort in **1648**. Aurangzeb's age added the **Moti Masjid** and the **Taj of the Deccan**. The style ended with **Safdarjung**'s tomb and **Asaf-ud-Daula**'s Bara Imambara. Builders used the **squinch** to set domes on squares, and **foreshortening** for lettering.

#### Monuments and builders

| Monument / device | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque** | Oldest mosque in India — temple material (Aibak) |
| **Qutub Minar** | Begun by Aibak, completed by Iltutmish |
| **Alai Darwaza (1311)** | First true arch and dome — Alauddin Khalji |
| **Tughlaqabad / Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's tomb** | Sloping (battered) walls |
| **Hauz Khas complex** | Firoz Shah Tughlaq's madrasa and reservoir |
| **Khirki Masjid** | Named for its perforated windows |
| **Atala Masjid, Jaunpur** | Sharqi dynasty |
| **Hoshang Shah's tomb, Mandu** | First marble tomb — precursor of the Taj |
| **Adina Mosque, Pandua** | Largest mosque of the Bengal Sultanate |
| **Madrasa at Bidar** | Mahmud Gawan (Bahmani) |
| **Mecca Masjid, Hyderabad** | Granite; begun 1617 (Qutb Shahi), completed 1694 |
| **Golconda fort** | Acoustic system; diamond trade |
| **Humayun's tomb** | Mirak Mirza Ghiyas — double dome, garden tomb |
| **Buland Darwaza** | Akbar's Gujarat victory (Fatehpur Sikri) |
| **Panch Mahal** | Five-storeyed pavilion, Fatehpur Sikri |
| **Itmad-ud-Daulah's tomb** | 'Baby Taj' — Nur Jahan; early pietra dura |
| **Taj Mahal — architect** | Ustad Ahmad Lahori |
| **Red Fort, Delhi** | Shah Jahan, completed 1648 |
| **Moti Masjid (Red Fort, Delhi)** | Aurangzeb's private mosque |
| **Bibi ka Maqbara** | 'Taj of the Deccan' — Aurangabad |
| **Safdarjung's tomb** | Last great Mughal garden tomb |
| **Bara Imambara, Lucknow** | Asaf-ud-Daula; famine relief; beamless hall |
| **Squinch / pendentive** | Round dome on a square base |
| **Foreshortening** | High inscriptions look as close as low ones |

**Don't confuse**
- **Alai Darwaza** = first **true** arch; earlier Sultanate arches (Quwwat-ul-Islam screen) were corbelled.
- **Bibi ka Maqbara** = 'Taj of the Deccan'; **Itmad-ud-Daulah** = 'Baby Taj'.
- **Moti Masjid, Red Fort** = Aurangzeb; **Moti Masjid, Agra Fort** = Shah Jahan.

**TL;DR**
- Sultanate: Quwwat-ul-Islam, Qutub Minar (Iltutmish), Alai Darwaza (first true arch), Tughlaq sloping walls, Hauz Khas, Khirki.
- Provincial: Sharqi Atala, Hoshang Shah's marble tomb, Adina; Deccan: Mahmud Gawan madrasa, Mecca Masjid, Golconda acoustics.
- Mughal: Humayun's tomb (Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, double dome), Buland Darwaza, Panch Mahal, Baby Taj, Taj (Ahmad Lahori), Red Fort 1648.
- Late: Moti Masjid, Bibi ka Maqbara, Safdarjung, Bara Imambara; squinch, foreshortening.
keyPoints: The Alai Darwaza has the first true arch in India.
Hoshang Shah's tomb at Mandu is the first marble tomb in India.
Humayun's tomb was designed by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas.
Bibi ka Maqbara is called the 'Taj of the Deccan'.
The Taj Mahal was designed by Ustad Ahmad Lahori.

items.title: Painting — From Bhimbetka to the Progressives
items.body:
### Painting — From Bhimbetka to the Progressives

**In one line**
The theory, the manuscript and miniature schools, the modern movements and the folk and tribal paintings with their states.

**The story**
Theory begins with Vatsyayana's **Shadanga**. The rock art of Bhimbetka is mostly **Mesolithic**. Manuscript art followed — Buddhist **Pala** palm leaves and the Jain **Kalpasutra** of the Apabhramsa school. Akbar's studio made the **Hamzanama**, and Jahangir's **Mansur** painted birds. Rajasthan gave Kishangarh's **Bani Thani**, and the Pahari hills gave **Basohli** and **Kangra**. The Deccan painted **Ragamala** sets. Modern art came with **Ravi Varma**'s oils and Abanindranath's **Bharat Mata**. In 1947 the **Progressive Artists** broke away, and Raza later painted his **Bindu** series. Folk painting is regional. Bengal has **Kalighat**, Maharashtra **Warli** and Bihar **Madhubani**. Odisha has Pattachitra (**Raghurajpur**) and **Saura**. Rajasthan has **Phad** and **Pichwai**; Central India has **Gond**. Karnataka has **Chittara**, UP **Sanjhi** and Telangana **Cheriyal**.

#### Painting

| School / work | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Shadanga** | Six limbs of painting — Vatsyayana's Kamasutra |
| **Bhimbetka rock paintings** | 500+ paintings, mostly Mesolithic |
| **Pala school** | Buddhist palm-leaf manuscripts |
| **Apabhramsa school** | Jain texts — Kalpasutra |
| **Hamzanama** | Akbar's atelier — Mir Sayyid Ali, Abd al-Samad |
| **Ustad Mansur** | Jahangir's painter of birds and animals |
| **Bani Thani** | Kishangarh — 'Indian Mona Lisa' |
| **Basohli** | Bold-coloured Pahari school |
| **Kangra** | Pahari — Gita Govinda themes |
| **Deccani school** | Bijapur Ragamala; Golconda portraits |
| **Abanindranath Tagore** | Bengal School — 'Bharat Mata' |
| **Progressive Artists' Group (1947)** | F.N. Souza, M.F. Husain, S.H. Raza |
| **S.H. Raza** | 'Bindu' series |
| **Raja Ravi Varma** | Oil paintings and lithographs (Kilimanoor) |
| **Kalighat painting** | Bengal, 19th c. — bold, satirical |
| **Warli painting** | Maharashtra — white rice paste on mud |
| **Madhubani painting** | Mithila, Bihar |
| **Pattachitra** | Odisha — Raghurajpur |
| **Phad painting** | Rajasthan scrolls (Pabuji) |
| **Pichwai** | Nathdwara — Krishna hangings |
| **Gond art** | Madhya Pradesh / Chhattisgarh |
| **Saura painting** | Odisha ritual wall art |
| **Chittara** | Karnataka — geometric patterns on red |
| **Sanjhi** | Paper-cutting art, Uttar Pradesh |
| **Cheriyal scrolls** | Telangana (Nakashi) scroll painting |

**Don't confuse**
- The source PDF says Mughal painting peaked under **Akbar**; the standard view (and our notes) is that it reached its **zenith under Jahangir** — Akbar founded the atelier (Hamzanama).
- **Pattachitra** = Odisha (Raghurajpur); **Phad** = Rajasthan; **Cheriyal** = Telangana; **Kalamkari** = Andhra Pradesh (see AP culture).

**TL;DR**
- Shadanga (Kamasutra); Bhimbetka mostly Mesolithic; Pala palm-leaf; Apabhramsa Kalpasutra.
- Mughal: Hamzanama (Akbar), Mansur (Jahangir); Rajput: Bani Thani; Pahari: Basohli, Kangra; Deccani Ragamala.
- Modern: Ravi Varma; Bengal School (Bharat Mata); Progressive Artists' Group 1947 (Souza, Husain, Raza — Bindu).
- Folk: Kalighat, Warli, Madhubani, Pattachitra (Raghurajpur), Phad, Pichwai, Gond, Saura, Chittara, Sanjhi, Cheriyal.
keyPoints: Vatsyayana's Kamasutra lists the six limbs (shadanga) of painting.
Bani Thani of the Kishangarh school is called the 'Indian Mona Lisa'.
Abanindranath Tagore painted 'Bharat Mata'.
Warli painting belongs to Maharashtra.
Pattachitra of Odisha is centred at Raghurajpur.

### Colonial and Modern Buildings and Their Architects — Detail

**In one line**
Name the architect: the Portuguese, French and British landmarks and the post-1947 buildings that exams pair with their designers.

**The story**
The Portuguese left the Sé Cathedral with its **Golden Bell**, Bom Jesus with St **Francis Xavier**'s relics, and Diu Fort (**1535**). The French built '**faceless**' plain facades. British Indo-Gothic gave **William Emerson**'s Victoria Memorial, **George Wittet**'s Gateway and **Stevens**'s CSMT. Indo-Saracenic began with the **Chepauk** Palace, and **Henry Irwin** worked at Shimla and Mysore. Post-1911 New Delhi, the '**Rome of Hindustan**', has Lutyens' **India Gate** and Baker's circular Parliament (**1927**). The Supreme Court (1958) is **Deolalikar**'s. After 1947 came **Louis Kahn**'s IIM-A and **Fariborz Sahba**'s Lotus Temple. **Kengal Hanumanthaiah** built the Vidhana Soudha, **Joseph Allen Stein** the Habitat Centre and **Raj Rewal** the Hall of Nations. Correa's work includes the **Gandhi Smarak** museum and **Kanchanjunga** apartments. Laurie Baker is the **Gandhi of Indian Architecture**; **Gautam Sarabhai** built NID and **Kanvinde** IIT Kanpur. In 2018 **Doshi** won the first Indian **Pritzker**.

#### Colonial

|---|---|
| **Sé Cathedral, Goa** | Houses the Golden Bell (1619) |
| **Basilica of Bom Jesus** | Relics of St Francis Xavier (1605) |
| **Diu Fort** | Portuguese, 1535 |
| **French colonial facades** | 'Faceless' — plain, unornamented |
| **Victoria Memorial, Kolkata** | William Emerson, 1921 |
| **Gateway of India** | George Wittet, 1924 |
| **CSMT, Mumbai** | F.W. Stevens, 1887 |
| **Chepauk Palace** | First Indo-Saracenic building |
| **Henry Irwin** | Viceregal Lodge, Shimla (1888); Mysore Palace |
| **New Delhi (post-1911)** | 'Rome of Hindustan' |
| **India Gate** | Lutyens' First World War memorial |
| **Parliament House (circular)** | Herbert Baker, 1927 |
| **Supreme Court building (1958)** | Ganesh Bhikaji Deolalikar |

#### Modern

| Building / architect | Fact |
|---|---|
| **IIM Ahmedabad** | Louis Kahn |
| **Lotus Temple** | Fariborz Sahba, 1986 |
| **Vidhana Soudha** | Kengal Hanumanthaiah, 1956 |
| **India Habitat Centre** | Joseph Allen Stein |
| **Hall of Nations, Pragati Maidan** | Raj Rewal |
| **Gandhi Smarak Sangrahalaya** | Charles Correa, 1963 |
| **Kanchanjunga Apartments** | Charles Correa, Mumbai |
| **Laurie Baker** | 'Gandhi of Indian Architecture' |

**Don't confuse**
- The source PDF credits the Supreme Court building to Herbert Baker; it was designed by **Ganesh Bhikaji Deolalikar** (1958). Baker designed Parliament House (1927).
- **Victoria Memorial** = William Emerson; **Gateway of India** = George Wittet; **CSMT** = F.W. Stevens.

**TL;DR**
- Portuguese: Sé Cathedral (Golden Bell), Bom Jesus (St Francis Xavier), Diu Fort 1535; French "faceless" facades.
- British: Victoria Memorial (Emerson), Gateway (Wittet), CSMT (Stevens); Chepauk first Indo-Saracenic; Henry Irwin.
- New Delhi 'Rome of Hindustan': India Gate (Lutyens), Parliament (Baker 1927); Supreme Court (Deolalikar 1958).
- Modern: Kahn (IIM-A), Sahba (Lotus Temple), Hanumanthaiah (Vidhana Soudha), Stein, Rewal, Correa (Gandhi Smarak, Kanchanjunga), Sarabhai (NID), Kanvinde (IIT-K), Doshi (Pritzker 2018).
keyPoints: The Victoria Memorial was designed by William Emerson.
The Gateway of India was designed by George Wittet.
The Chepauk Palace is regarded as the first Indo-Saracenic building.

### Every Indian Cultural World Heritage Site and its Year

**In one line**
The full cultural list in order of inscription — the year is what exams ask.

**The story**
India's cultural sites were added in waves. **1983** brought Ajanta, Ellora, **Agra Fort** and the **Taj Mahal**, and **1984** brought **Konark** and **Mahabalipuram**. In **1986** came the **Churches and Convents of Goa**, **Khajuraho**, **Hampi** and **Fatehpur Sikri**; in **1987** **Pattadakal**, **Elephanta** and the **Great Living Chola Temples**. **Sanchi** followed in **1989**, and **Humayun's Tomb** and the **Qutb Minar** in **1993**. The **Mountain Railways** began in **1999**, then **Mahabodhi** (**2002**), **Bhimbetka** (**2003**), **Champaner** and **Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus** (**2004**). Later came the **Red Fort Complex** (**2007**), **Jantar Mantar** (**2010**), the **Hill Forts of Rajasthan** (**2013**) and **Rani-ki-Vav** (**2014**). **Nalanda** and the **Capitol Complex** came in **2016**, **Ahmedabad** in **2017**, Mumbai's **Art Deco** in **2018** and **Jaipur City** in **2019**. The Kakatiya **Rudreshwara** temple and **Dholavira** followed in **2021**; the later inscriptions (2023–2026) are in the UNESCO note above. Andhra's Lepakshi is on the **Tentative List**.

**Don't confuse**
- **Ramappa (2021)** is India's 39th site and is in **Telangana**, not AP; **Lepakshi** (AP) is only on the **Tentative List**.
- **CSMT (2004)** ≠ **Victorian Gothic & Art Deco Ensembles (2018)** — two separate Mumbai inscriptions.

**TL;DR**
- 1983 Ajanta, Ellora, Agra Fort, Taj; 1984 Konark, Mahabalipuram; 1986 Goa churches, Khajuraho, Hampi, Fatehpur Sikri.
- 1987 Pattadakal, Elephanta, Chola temples; 1989 Sanchi; 1993 Humayun's Tomb, Qutb; 1999 Mountain Railways.
- 2002 Mahabodhi; 2003 Bhimbetka; 2004 Champaner, CSMT; 2007 Red Fort; 2010 Jantar Mantar; 2013 Hill Forts; 2014 Rani-ki-Vav.
- 2016 Nalanda, Capitol Complex; 2017 Ahmedabad; 2018 Mumbai Art Deco; 2019 Jaipur; 2021 Ramappa, Dholavira; Lepakshi tentative.

items.body:
### For Mains — Indian Art & Architecture

**In one line**
For Mains Paper-II (M2-2b, fine arts), treat architecture not as a list of monuments but as evidence of synthesis, patronage and regional identity.

**How Mains frames this topic**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Evolution | trabeate temple forms (Nagara/Dravida/Vesara) → arcuate Indo-Islamic → colonial Indo-Saracenic/Neo-Classical → modern (Chandigarh) |
| Features | tower types, gopurams, charbagh, jaali, pietra dura, frescoes/miniatures |
| Significance | religion, royal legitimacy, economy of guilds, engineering (Kailasa monolith, Gol Gumbaz dome) |
| Synthesis | Indo-Islamic fusion; Qutb Shahi Deccani; Indo-Saracenic colonial revival |
| AP angle | Amaravati marble school, Nagarjunakonda, Lepakshi murals, Srisailam/Tirupati |
| Way forward | ASI conservation, UNESCO listing, heritage tourism, GI/craft linkage |

**Data points / examples to quote**
- Brihadeeswarar, Thanjavur (Rajaraja Chola I, c. 1010 CE) — UNESCO 'Great Living Chola Temples'.
- Kailasa Temple, Ellora — world's largest monolithic excavation (Rashtrakuta Krishna I).
- Taj Mahal and Humayun's Tomb — charbagh and pietra dura; India has 45 UNESCO sites (2026).
- Amaravati stupa's ayaka pillars — Andhra's unique Buddhist contribution.

**Use in answers**
- Open with a definition of style (trabeate vs arcuate) then argue 'synthesis, not imposition'.
- Diagram idea: a timeline bar from Mauryan rock-cut → temple styles → Indo-Islamic → colonial → modern.
- Quote: temple architecture as 'frozen music' / stone record of a dynasty's power.
- Always close an AP-flavoured answer with Amaravati, Lepakshi and the Kakatiya Ramappa (UNESCO 2021).

**TL;DR**
- Argue evolution → features → significance → synthesis → AP angle → conservation.
- Keep 4–5 dated examples ready (Brihadeeswarar, Kailasa, Taj, Amaravati, Ramappa).
- The reliable thesis is 'Indian architecture is a story of synthesis and patronage'.
keyPoints: Mains clause M2-2b (Paper-II) — fine arts within AP medieval culture; frame architecture as synthesis + patronage.
Structure answers as evolution → features → significance → synthesis → AP angle → conservation.
Quote dated anchors: Brihadeeswarar (c.1010), Kailasa (Krishna I), Taj Mahal, Amaravati ayaka pillars.
AP angle: Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Lepakshi, Ramappa (UNESCO 2021), Srisailam/Tirupati.
Way forward: ASI conservation, UNESCO listing, heritage tourism and craft/GI linkage.
